subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to Hadith, the first of a person’s deeds to be examined on the Day of Judgement will be:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said the first deed for which a servant will be held accountable is his prayer (Tirmidhi, Nasa’i).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Adhan was introduced:
explanation: After the Hijrah, when Muslims could pray openly in congregation, the Adhan was adopted as the call to prayer.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The phrase ‘Prayer is better than sleep’ is added to the Adhan of:
explanation: In the Fajr Adhan the words “As-salatu khairum min-an-naum” are added because people are asleep at dawn.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The call given immediately before the congregational prayer begins is called:
explanation: The Iqamah is the second call, given just before the Imam begins the prayer, signalling the congregation to stand.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: On Friday, the Jumu‘ah prayer is offered in place of:
explanation: Jumu‘ah, with its Khutbah, replaces the Zuhr prayer for those who attend it.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The voluntary prayer offered in the latter part of the night after sleeping is called:
explanation: The Qur’an (Surah Al-Isra and Al-Muzzammil) urges night prayer; Tahajjud is offered after rising from sleep.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The special night prayer offered in congregation during Ramadan is called:
explanation: Tarawih is prayed after Isha in the nights of Ramadan; its name comes from the short rests taken between sets of rak‘ahs.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The prayer offered to seek rain from Allah is called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) led people out to an open ground to pray for rain in times of drought; this is Salat-ul-Istisqa.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Salat-ul-Kusuf is offered on the occasion of:
explanation: When the sun eclipsed, the Prophet (PBUH) led a long prayer and taught that eclipses are signs of Allah, not linked to anyone’s death or birth.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The prayer offered to seek Allah’s guidance before making a decision is called:
explanation: Istikharah means seeking what is good; the Prophet (PBUH) taught a supplication for it after two rak‘ahs.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The voluntary prayer offered in the forenoon, after the sun has risen well, is called:
explanation: Salat-ud-Duha (Chasht) is prayed in the late morning; the Prophet (PBUH) encouraged it in several Hadith.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: What type of Prayer is Namaz-e-Janaza?
explanation: The funeral prayer is a collective obligation: if some Muslims perform it, the rest are absolved, but if none do, all are sinful.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which prayer is offered without Ruku and Sajdah?
explanation: The funeral prayer is offered standing with takbirs, supplications and salam, without bowing or prostration.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The prostrations made at the end of Salah to make up for an unintentional mistake are called:
explanation: Sahw means forgetfulness; two extra prostrations compensate for certain omissions or additions made by mistake.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The prostration performed on reciting or hearing certain verses of the Qur’an is called:
explanation: At particular verses that mention prostration, the reciter and listener perform a Sajdah of recitation.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Purification with clean earth when water is unavailable or harmful is called:
explanation: The Qur’an permits Tayammum with clean earth when water cannot be found or used, showing the ease of Islamic law.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Wiping over leather socks instead of washing the feet in ablution is called:
explanation: Authentic Sunnah allows wiping over leather socks worn in a state of purity, for a limited period.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The ritual bath of the whole body is called:
explanation: Ghusl removes major ritual impurity and is required, for example, after marital relations and at the end of menstruation.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The state of minor ritual impurity, removed by Wudu, is called:
explanation: Hadath-e-Asghar (e.g. after sleep or answering the call of nature) requires Wudu; Hadath-e-Akbar such as Janabat requires Ghusl.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: ‘Qasr’ in Salah means:
o: Combining two prayers at one time
Shortening four-rak‘ah obligatory prayers during a journey
explanation: A traveller offers two rak‘ahs instead of four in Zuhr, Asr and Isha; this concession is called Qasr.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Offering an obligatory prayer after its prescribed time has passed is called:
explanation: Ada is performance within the prescribed time, while Qada is making up a missed obligation afterwards.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A worshipper who joins the congregation after one or more rak‘ahs have been completed is called:
explanation: A Masbuq completes the missed rak‘ahs after the Imam’s salam; a Munfarid prays alone.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The opening ‘Allahu Akbar’ with which Salah formally begins is called:
explanation: It is called Tahrimah because with it ordinary speech and actions become forbidden until the prayer ends.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The testimony recited in the sitting position of Salah, beginning ‘At-Tahiyyatu lillah’, is called:
explanation: The Tashahhud contains the testimony of faith and is recited in the sitting posture of Salah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Fasting in Ramadan was made obligatory in:
explanation: The verses of Surah Al-Baqarah ordaining the fast of Ramadan were revealed in Madinah in the second year of the Hijrah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to the Qur’an, the main purpose of fasting is to attain:
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah says fasting was prescribed “so that you may attain Taqwa” (God-consciousness).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The pre-dawn meal taken before beginning a fast is called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said, “Take Suhur, for in it there is blessing” (Bukhari).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Staying in the mosque for worship, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan, is called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) regularly observed I‘tikaf in the last ten days of Ramadan, devoting himself fully to worship.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) advised seeking Laylat-ul-Qadr in:
o: The first ten nights of Ramadan
The odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan
explanation: Sahih al-Bukhari reports the instruction to seek the Night of Decree in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An elderly person permanently unable to fast is required to pay:
explanation: The Qur’an allows those who cannot fast to feed a poor person for each day missed; this compensation is Fidyah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to Hadith, the gate of Paradise reserved for those who fast is called:
explanation: Bukhari and Muslim report that Paradise has a gate called Ar-Rayyan through which only those who fast will enter.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Fasting is forbidden on which days?
o: The Day of Arafah and Ashura
The last day of Sha‘ban and Rajab
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) forbade fasting on the two Eids, which are days of celebration and thanks.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Continuous fasting without breaking the fast at sunset, which the Prophet (PBUH) forbade his followers, is called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) discouraged Wisal for his Ummah out of mercy, saying he was not like them in this.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The voluntary fast observed by the Holy Prophet (PBUH) on the 10th of Muharram is known as the fast of:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) fasted on the day of Ashura and encouraged it; the day marked the deliverance of Musa (AS) from Pharaoh.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Fasting on the Day of Arafah (9th Dhul-Hijjah) is especially recommended for:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) praised the Arafah fast for those not on Hajj, while he himself did not fast at Arafat so pilgrims could devote themselves to worship.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The six voluntary fasts kept after Eid-ul-Fitr are observed in the month of:
explanation: Sahih Muslim reports that fasting Ramadan followed by six days of Shawwal is like fasting the whole year.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hajj is performed in the month of:
explanation: The main rites of Hajj take place from the 8th to the 13th of Dhul-Hijjah, the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The sacred state, with its prescribed dress, that a pilgrim enters for Hajj or Umrah is called:
explanation: On entering Ihram, the pilgrim wears simple garments and avoids acts such as cutting hair, using perfume and hunting.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The words ‘Labbaik Allahumma Labbaik’ recited by pilgrims are called:
explanation: The Talbiyah, “Here I am, O Allah, here I am”, is recited from assuming Ihram until the pilgrim begins stoning on the 10th.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which rite is described in a Hadith as the essence of Hajj (‘Hajj is Arafah’)?
explanation: Standing at Arafat on the 9th of Dhul-Hijjah is the central pillar of Hajj; missing it means missing Hajj.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Circumambulation of the Ka‘bah is called:
explanation: Tawaf consists of seven circuits around the Ka‘bah, beginning from the Black Stone.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Sa‘i between Safa and Marwah commemorates:
o: Hazrat Ibrahim’s (AS) building of the Ka‘bah
explanation: Pilgrims walk between the two hills as Hajira did while searching for water for Isma‘il (AS), before Zamzam gushed forth.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Throwing pebbles at the pillars at Mina during Hajj is called:
explanation: Ramy recalls Ibrahim (AS) rejecting Satan’s temptation and symbolises the rejection of evil.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The 8th of Dhul-Hijjah, when pilgrims proceed to Mina, is called:
explanation: Tarwiyah refers to pilgrims providing themselves with water before setting out; the Hajj days begin on this date.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The 10th of Dhul-Hijjah, the day of sacrifice, is called:
explanation: Nahr means slaughter; on this day pilgrims stone the large pillar, sacrifice, shave and perform Tawaf-e-Ziyarat.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The fixed points at which pilgrims must enter the state of Ihram are called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) fixed Mawaqit for people coming from different directions; pilgrims may not cross them without Ihram.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Pilgrims from Pakistan and the Indian subcontinent travelling by the southern sea route traditionally assume Ihram at the Miqat of:
explanation: Yalamlam is the Miqat fixed for people coming from Yemen and the south, the direction from which subcontinental pilgrims approached by sea.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The type of Hajj in which Umrah is performed first, Ihram is taken off, and a fresh Ihram is assumed for Hajj is:
explanation: In Tamattu‘ the pilgrim enjoys release from Ihram between Umrah and Hajj; Qiran combines both in one Ihram and Ifrad is Hajj alone.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which of the following is NOT a rite of Umrah?
explanation: Umrah consists of Ihram, Tawaf, Sa‘i and cutting the hair; standing at Arafat belongs only to Hajj.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: After leaving Arafat, pilgrims spend the night at:
explanation: Pilgrims combine Maghrib and Isha at Muzdalifah, spend the night there and collect pebbles before returning to Mina.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The obligatory Tawaf of Hajj, performed after returning from Arafat and Muzdalifah, is called:
explanation: Tawaf-e-Ziyarat is a pillar of Hajj; Tawaf-e-Qudum is the arrival Tawaf and Tawaf-e-Wida‘ the farewell Tawaf.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Kissing, touching or gesturing towards the Black Stone during Tawaf is called:
explanation: Istilam of Hajr-e-Aswad marks the start of each circuit; Ramal is brisk walking and Idtiba‘ baring the right shoulder.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Maqam-e-Ibrahim is:
o: The stone on which Ibrahim (AS) stood while building the Ka‘bah
explanation: The Qur’an commands, “Take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer”; two rak‘ahs are prayed there after Tawaf.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The well of Zamzam is associated with:
explanation: Zamzam gushed forth for the infant Isma‘il (AS) and his mother Hajira in the barren valley of Makkah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Standing shoulder to shoulder in congregational prayer chiefly symbolises:
o: The equality and brotherhood of believers
explanation: Rich and poor, ruler and subject stand in the same rows, showing that only piety distinguishes people before Allah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to Surah Al-Ankabut, Salah:
explanation: The Qur’an says prayer restrains from shameful and evil deeds, showing its moral purpose.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Pilgrims of every nation and class wearing identical simple garments in Hajj chiefly demonstrates:
o: The wealth of the Muslim world
The equality and unity of the Ummah
explanation: The Ihram removes marks of rank and wealth, presenting the Ummah as one brotherhood before Allah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An important social effect of fasting is that it:
o: Develops empathy with the hungry and poor
explanation: Experiencing hunger and thirst makes the fasting person feel the hardship of the poor and encourages generosity.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Qur’anic statement that Salah is prescribed at fixed times chiefly teaches:
explanation: Surah An-Nisa describes prayer as an obligation at fixed times; offering it on time five times a day trains discipline.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islam, ‘Ibadah’ is understood to include:
o: Only acts performed in a mosque
Every lawful act done with the intention of pleasing Allah
explanation: Islam regards all of life as worship when lawful acts are done sincerely for Allah, not only formal rituals.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to Surah Adh-Dhariyat, jinn and mankind were created to:
explanation: Allah says, “I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Qur’an (Surah Ar-Ra‘d) states that hearts find rest in:
explanation: “Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest”; Dhikr gives inner peace and contentment.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The intention made before an act of worship is called:
explanation: Niyyah distinguishes worship from habit; the Hadith says actions are judged by intentions.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A single unit of Salah, consisting of standing, bowing and prostration, is called:
explanation: Each prayer consists of a set number of rak‘ahs; Qiyam, Ruku and Sajdah are postures within a rak‘ah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Surah Al-Mu’minun praises believers who are humble and attentive in their prayers. This quality is called:
explanation: Khushu‘ is humility and concentration of heart and body in Salah; the Surah begins with it among the traits of successful believers.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A supplication recited while standing in prayer, as in Witr, is called:
explanation: Du‘a-e-Qunut is recited in the standing position; Thana is the opening praise recited at the start of Salah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An object placed in front of a person praying, marking a boundary others should not cross, is called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) prayed facing a Sutrah such as a spear or staff and forbade passing in front of one who is praying.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The two rak‘ahs offered on entering a mosque before sitting down are called:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said that whoever enters the mosque should pray two rak‘ahs before sitting (Bukhari, Muslim).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The person who calls the Adhan is called:
explanation: The Mu’adhdhin calls believers to prayer; the Imam leads it and the Khatib delivers the sermon.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Unlike the Jumu‘ah prayer, in the Eid prayer the Khutbah is delivered:
explanation: In Jumu‘ah the sermon precedes the prayer, but in both Eid prayers the Prophet (PBUH) prayed first and then delivered the Khutbah.
